newsitem.title: USA: Tungsten scrap tightness boosts concentrates, APT.
newsitem.headline: Tungsten scrap tightness boosts concentrates, APT.

text.p: Tungsten scrap prices have risen sharply as supplies dwindle, causing some consumers to dip into stocks of concentrates and ammonium paratungstate (APT), industry sources said.

"The consumption of virgin tungsten has climbed quite strongly in the last few weeks. Hard scrap prices have soared and people who normally use it have to buy more virgin material," said Robert Bunting of tungsten producer Avocet Mining plc.
Tungsten is essential in cutting tools and drill bits, as well as light bulb filaments, and defense materials.
A U.S. tungsten scrap merchant said tungsten carbide scrap and pure tungsten stockpiles in Russia and elsewhere in the former Soviet Union have largely been depleted.
"No new scrap is being generated there, and the demand for scrap is much higher than it used to be," the merchant said.
Bunting said tungsten consumption is also picking up with additional offtake in Japan especially, and in Europe to a lesser extent.
The scrap gap was being filled by eating into Western stockpiles of concentrates and APT in Rotterdam and elsewhere, Bunting said. Russian stocks were falling and domestic offtake was rising.
"These surplus piles are suddenly being attacked, but the replenishment of these inventories is not there," Bunting added.
Stockpiles have been crucial in plugging the production deficit in recent years, Bunting said. Low tungsten prices have shuttered some Western production capacity.

Tungsten scrap prices have also gathered some momentum from the run-up in cobalt, and the confused state of that market amid an indefinite postponement of U.S. Stockpile sales, and civil war in Zaire, a major producer, industry sources said.
Tungsten scrap contains 6.5 to 18 percent cobalt, depending on form.
A U.S. tungsten consumer said scrap prices have risen some 15 percent in recent weeks as the shortage bites, though there was no lack of concentrates or ore.
"I think the scrap market is quite confused because a lot of people who are generators of scrap are holding material in anticipation it will be worth more in a month or so," the consumer said.

The consumer dismissed suggestions that Russian stockpiles of tungsten have run dry. "I am seeing more stockpiled material being offered than ever before. I am not of the opinion stockpiles are running out," he said.
Bunting estimated that consumption this year will be 40,000 to 41,000 tonnes of contained tungsten in virgin materials, and a further 8,000 to 9,000 tonnes of recycled metal.
He pegged standard concentrates prices at $45-$55 per metric tonne unit.
